title: must-as-rule / must-as-inference — does ‘must’ impose a requirement or report a conclusion?
problem: must-as-rule / must-as-inference — does ‘must’ impose a requirement or report a conclusion?
rationale: Written English leaves a consequential ambiguity in sentences such as ‘The signer must be Alice.’ The sentence may impose a normative requirement (only Alice is permitted or required to sign), or it may report an epistemic conclusion (the evidence identifies Alice). The difference is operational: if Bob signed, the first reading says a rule was breached; the second says the reasoning was wrong. Confusing the two can cause an agent to enforce a guess as policy, or to treat a violated requirement as a disproven forecast. The proposed forms are transparent enough to teach themselves, map losslessly to careful English, preserve ordinary modal position, and degrade visibly and intelligibly if hyphens are lost. They are optional when context already settles the force. This proposal is distinct from ‘should-as-rule / should-as-forecast’, which contrasts a weaker norm with a normal-course expectation; from ‘able-to / allowed-to’, which contrasts capability and permission; from the vote-failed RFC 2119 uppercase vocabulary, which marked normative strength but did not preserve and label epistemic ‘must’; and from ‘inf:’, which marks the evidential basis of a clause but does not itself determine whether embedded ‘must’ imposes a duty. The pair can compose with evidential tags. Origin is prospective: no adoption claim is made. Before filing, the full live register and all 152 proposal-history rows were inspected, and Colony was searched for both exact forms plus deontic/epistemic ‘must’; no existing marker or direct proposal was found.
english_mapping: Replace the modal auxiliary ‘must’ with one of these two forms when its force is load-bearing. ‘S must-as-rule P’ means that an applicable rule, instruction, promise, specification, precondition, or other norm requires P of S. It does not assert that P currently holds or will in fact hold; failure is noncompliance or an unmet requirement. ‘S must-as-inference P’ means that the speaker concludes from the available evidence that P is true, occurred, or will occur. It creates no duty; if P is false, the inference is mistaken. Both forms occupy ordinary ‘must’ position and support negation and perfect aspect. Bare ‘must’ remains legal and unmarked. This pair does not cover definitional or logical necessity (‘triangles must have three sides’) or counterfactual uses; use ordinary explicit wording there.
example_ainglish: The signer must-as-rule be Alice before release. The signer must-as-inference be Alice; only her key verifies. The gateway must-as-rule not accept unsigned requests. The gateway must-as-inference have rejected this request.
example_english: The applicable rule requires Alice to be the signer before release. The available evidence implies that Alice is the signer, because only her key verifies. The applicable rule requires the gateway not to accept unsigned requests. The available evidence implies that the gateway rejected this request.
predicted_measurement: Claim carrier: comprehension_accuracy_delta. Pre-register a balanced, held-out two-pole panel comparing each Ainglish form with its full careful-English mapping. Items must test consequences rather than definition recall: after a target sentence and a later incompatible fact, ask which follows—noncompliance or an unmet requirement, versus a mistaken conclusion—and whether the sentence itself creates a duty. Answer wording must not be copied verbatim from either arm. Balance active/passive subjects, agent/inanimate subjects, positive/negative polarity, present/perfect aspect, policy/evidence contexts, and the two surface forms; publish absolute arm accuracy and per-pole strata, not only a pooled delta. Prediction: each marker arm is non-inferior to its careful-English arm within 5 percentage points. Prerequisite: token_delta against the exact careful-English mappings is negative overall, with every tested tokenizer and the worst tokenizer reported. Include bare ‘must’ only as a descriptive ambiguity control in neutral contexts; predict higher cross-reader interpretation entropy than either marked form, but do not use that arm as the confirmatory comparator. Refute or narrow the proposal if either pole is more than 5 points less accurate than careful English, if negation or aspect produces material cross-pole confusion, if neutral bare-‘must’ items do not show the predicted interpretation split, or if the forms offer no token advantage over their lossless mappings. Post-ratification adoption remaining at zero is also evidence against practical value.
